Assistant-written selective paraphrase of UMN Extension: Monstera deliciosa. Accessed 2026-09-08. This is an abridged summary, not a quotation or complete captured page.
Source: https://extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/propagating-monstera-deliciosa

For Monstera deliciosa, a propagating stem piece needs a node with an axillary bud; a detached leaf or petiole alone cannot develop into a new growing plant. Rooting medium should provide moisture and physical support while draining well. Monstera can root in plain water or suitable solid media. Additional rooting hormone is optional; it can speed rooting but is not required. Inspect roots before moving a cutting: a piece with few or no roots should remain in its rooting medium. Healthy roots are firm and creamy white; soft brown roots suggest excessive moisture or poor drainage. Healthy roots together with active growth indicate readiness for a longer-term pot. These recommendations concern Monstera cuttings, not every plant species. The page describes several propagation and care methods rather than one universally necessary method.

Source: https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/propagating-houseplants

Propagation methods differ with a plant’s structure and growth habit. Stem cuttings suit pothos, whereas leaf propagation suits African violets. Iowa State lists leaf cuttings and division for snake plant, and stem cuttings and layering for Monstera deliciosa. These are recommended methods, not a proof that every unlisted approach is biologically impossible.

Source: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/a-an-and-the

Article choice depends on what the listener or reader can identify and on the noun’s use. A or an introduces a singular countable referent that is not already identifiable to that audience; the identifies a referent recoverable from shared knowledge or context. A previous mention is one way to establish reference, not the only one. A and an are limited to singular countable uses, and their form follows the next spoken sound rather than its written first letter. The can accompany singular, plural or uncountable nouns when a particular referent is intended. Bare plural and uncountable nouns commonly express general classes or substances; the can pick out a particular set or amount. Some singular generic uses also take the, so generic meaning is not a universal prohibition. Article use changes with context and intended reference, not just the noun’s spelling.

Article choice depends on what the listener or reader can identify and on the noun’s use. A or an introduces a singular countable referent that is not already identifiable to that audience; the identifies a referent recoverable from shared knowledge or context. A previous mention is one way to establish reference, not the only one. A and an are limited to singular countable uses, and their form follows the next spoken sound rather than its written first letter. The can accompany singular, plural or uncountable nouns when a particular referent is intended. Bare plural and uncountable nouns commonly express general classes or substances; the can pick out a particular set or amount. Some singular generic uses also take the, so generic meaning is not a universal prohibition. Article use changes with context and intended reference, not just the noun’s spelling.

Source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-I19-PURL-gpo183480/pdf/GOVPUB-I19-PURL-gpo183480.pdf

Topographic contours connect locations at the same elevation relative to a reference surface. Labeled, heavier index contours help establish elevations; intermediate contours provide additional terrain detail. The contour interval describes a vertical elevation difference, not horizontal travel distance, and is given in the map margin. On the same map, tightly spaced ordinary contours represent steeper terrain, whereas wider spacing represents gentler terrain. A map’s chosen interval depends on its terrain, so maps can use different intervals. Labels identify elevation, while spacing helps describe how rapidly elevation changes over horizontal distance. Map legends distinguish ordinary, supplementary and depression contours and other symbols; their meaning must be read using the relevant legend. This summary concerns contour interpretation, not an assertion that a mapped route is safe or passable.

Source: https://extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/propagating-monstera-deliciosa

For Monstera deliciosa, a propagating stem piece needs a node with an axillary bud; a detached leaf or petiole alone cannot develop into a new growing plant. Rooting medium should provide moisture and physical support while draining well. Monstera can root in plain water or suitable solid media. Additional rooting hormone is optional; it can speed rooting but is not required. Inspect roots before moving a cutting: a piece with few or no roots should remain in its rooting medium. Healthy roots are firm and creamy white; soft brown roots suggest excessive moisture or poor drainage. Healthy roots together with active growth indicate readiness for a longer-term pot. These recommendations concern Monstera cuttings, not every plant species. The page describes several propagation and care methods rather than one universally necessary method.

sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective paraphrase of Cambridge English Grammar Today: A/an and the. Accessed 2026-09-08. This is an abridged summary, not a quotation or complete captured page.
Source: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/a-an-and-the

Article choice depends on what the listener or reader can identify and on the noun’s use. A or an introduces a singular countable referent that is not already identifiable to that audience; the identifies a referent recoverable from shared knowledge or context. A previous mention is one way to establish reference, not the only one. A and an are limited to singular countable uses, and their form follows the next spoken sound rather than its written first letter. The can accompany singular, plural or uncountable nouns when a particular referent is intended. Bare plural and uncountable nouns commonly express general classes or substances; the can pick out a particular set or amount. Some singular generic uses also take the, so generic meaning is not a universal prohibition. Article use changes with context and intended reference, not just the noun’s spelling.

questions.prompt: A travel blog opens: "We arrived in Lisbon and checked into ___ hotel near the river. ___ staff were welcoming, and ___ breakfast included fresh pastries." Which articles complete the passage to show first introduction, then shared reference, then a general class?
choices: a / The / (no article)
the / A / the
an / The / a
the / The / the
questions.explanation: The first blank needs "a" because the hotel is newly introduced and not yet identifiable. The second blank needs "The" because "staff" now refers to the specific people at that hotel, recoverable from context. The third blank needs no article (bare "breakfast") because it names a general class of meal included, not a particular instance being singled out.

questions.prompt: In a recipe comment, someone writes: "I substituted ___ honey for sugar, but ___ honey I used was too strong." What explains the article shift between the two mentions?
questions.expectedAnswer: First: general substance; second: specific instance now known from context
choices: First: general substance; second: specific instance now known from context
First: countable singular; second: plural noun
First: shared reference; second: first introduction
First: any amount; second: uncountable prohibition
questions.explanation: The first "honey" has no article because it names the general substance (any honey, uncountable class). The second takes "the" because it refers to the particular honey the commenter actually used, now identifiable from the shared context of their specific substitution. The shift tracks when the referent becomes contextually recoverable, not when the noun repeats.
questions.topic: specific versus general meaning and countability

questions.prompt: A travel blog opens with: "We arrived in Paris and checked into a hotel near the river. The view from the room was spectacular." Why does the second sentence use "the" for both "view" and "room"?
questions.expectedAnswer: Both nouns refer back to specific items established in the previous sentence.
choices: Both nouns refer back to specific items established in the previous sentence.
The writer uses "the" for any noun following a proper noun like "Paris."
"View" and "room" are uncountable nouns that require "the."
The article "the" indicates these are generic statements about all hotel rooms.
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces "a hotel" as new information, making it identifiable. "The room" refers specifically to the room in that hotel—now shared, identifiable context. "The view" is similarly tied to that specific room's perspective. Both nouns shift from indefinite to definite because the preceding sentence established shared reference; the reader can now identify which room and which view are meant.

questions.prompt: Two trails each gain 100 m in elevation. Trail A crosses 5 contour lines over 1 km; Trail B crosses 5 contour lines over 2 km. The map's contour interval is 20 m. Which comparison is correct?
questions.expectedAnswer: Both trails have equal total elevation gain, but Trail B has a gentler slope.
choices: Both trails have equal total elevation gain, but Trail B has a gentler slope.
Trail A has greater elevation gain and a steeper slope.
Both trails have equal total elevation gain, but Trail A has a gentler slope.

questions.explanation: Each trail crosses 5 intervals × 20 m = 100 m total elevation gain, confirming the stated gain. Trail A's slope: 100 m / 1,000 m = 1:10.
